problem: Autonomous valet parking (AVP) systems depend on pre-built HD/vectorized maps and only execute predefined tasks, while existing zero-shot VLN and VLM-based driving methods do not fit enclosed underground garages or kinematically constrained vehicles, and there is no VLN benchmark for underground parking.
motivation: Map-free AVP that follows natural-language instructions (e.g. 'park near the elevator lobby') requires semantic understanding of signs and markings. Single-frame, low-frequency VLM reasoning misses transient cues such as signs seen briefly, and repeated queries are costly and unstable, so memory is needed.
key_idea: Combine MapTR BEV candidate trajectories with a zero-shot VLM, augmented by a short-term sign-detection memory and a long-term topological memory, inside a hierarchical decision module that picks kinematically feasible trajectories.
insight: Both memories help: removing LTM lowers regular-task SR from 65.2 to 56.8, and further removing STM lowers it to 42.2. STM raises semantic cue identification from 57.7% to 84.6% at critical junctions. LTM cuts VLM calls from 1403 to 317 and cost from $1.06 to $0.24 over 10 episodes, and SR and the SR/OSR ratio grow over 50 attempts in one scene. Kinematically feasible BEV trajectories matter: MapGPT with BEV goes from 9.3 to 37.6 SR over the original MapGPT.
method: BEV perception and candidate trajectories: MapTR on 4 surround cameras predicts lane centerlines; an optimizer with Reeds-Shepp curves and vehicle kinematics generates drivable candidate trajectories, which serve as the action space.

Short-term memory (STM): Grounding DINO with the prompt 'sign' on the front image runs at high frequency; a K=6 frame queue stores (annotated image, boxes, time, yaw) with object (IoU tracking), directional (yaw difference) and temporal filters.

VLM decision core: a target extractor splits the instruction into sub-goals; Gemini-3-flash receives the front image, STM images, system prompt and the current sub-goal and outputs forward/left/right/stop, cached in an action cache to decouple its latency from control.

Long-term topological memory (LTM): a directed graph with junction nodes, landmark nodes (stop points) and edges storing a direction vector (from the last 5 points) plus validity bits, updated from user feedback and system-triggered failures.

Hierarchical decision module: at junctions (≥2 candidates), first query LTM by graph search and choose the candidate whose direction has the highest cosine similarity with the next edge (above a threshold); otherwise map the latest cached VLM action to the candidate with the closest angle; then execute.

VLN-AVP dataset/benchmark: 10 real underground garages scanned with LiDAR and fisheye cameras, rendered by 3DGS in a Real2Sim2Real simulator extended from REAP; over 1000 episodes split into Regular and Challenging subsets.

setting.training_data: none for the navigation policy (zero-shot VLM); MapTR is used for BEV perception with no training details given
setting.observation: four surround-view RGB cameras (front camera used for the VLM and detection) plus vehicle yaw/pose
setting.action_space: meta-actions {forward, left, right, stop} mapped to candidate BEV trajectories executed by a low-level controller
setting.simulator: custom 3DGS-based Real2Sim2Real simulator (from REAP) with vehicle kinematics; plus a real vehicle
setting.privileged: none at test time (user feedback on success/failure is used to update the LTM)

numbers.extra: full method with STM + LTM; LTM is built up over episodes with user feedback

numbers_note: The split is not specified for the simulation benchmark; 'test' is used as a placeholder. The paper reports no standard-benchmark results (R2R etc.). The 50-attempt learning curve is shown only in a figure.
results: In simulation, VLN-AVP reaches 65.2 SR / 43.1 SPL on Regular tasks and 45.4 SR / 33.2 SPL on Challenging tasks, beating the strongest baseline LaMPilot (49.7 and 33.6 SR) and MapGPT w/ BEV. In the real world it reaches 63.3% SR versus 36.7% for LaMPilot (30 trials).
limitations: The VLM is weak at directional and spatial reasoning, and the authors plan additional training for it.
The LTM depends on user feedback and repeated visits, so its benefit is small with few episodes (real-world tests had only 30 trials); the real-world comparison covers only one baseline.
The dataset is not yet public; the sign-only detection prompt and reliance on a strong closed VLM (Gemini-3-flash) incur API cost and latency.
